# Parameters

Sixteen per modelling unit, plus `area_km2`, which is geometry rather than a
fitted quantity. `python -c "import dcrest; print(dcrest.params.describe())"`
prints this table from the code, so it cannot drift from the implementation.

<!-- AUTOGEN:parameters BEGIN -->
*Generated by `scripts/gen_parameter_table.py` — edit that file, not this table.*

### The 16 parameters

| name | units | range | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `tsnow` | degC | -2 … 3 | 0.5 | air temperature separating snow from rain |
| `ddf` | mm/degC/day | 1 … 8 | 3 | degree-day melt factor |
| `ft` | &mdash; | 0 … 0.7 | 0.1 | interception capacity as a fraction of `wm` |
| `wm` | mm | 1 … 2000 | 200 | mean soil-water capacity of the unit |
| `b` | &mdash; | 0.01 … 6 | 1 | shape of the capacity distribution (VIC curve) |
| `im` | &mdash; | 0 … 0.5 | 0.05 | impervious fraction |
| `ke` | &mdash; | 0.2 … 2.5 | 1 | multiplier on potential ET |
| `fc` | mm/h | 0 … 5 | 0.5 | saturated hydraulic conductivity; caps interflow |
| `ksoil` | 1/day | 0 … 0.5 | 0.05 | soil to aquifer drainage rate |
| `hmaxaq` | mm | 50 … 4000 | 500 | aquifer capacity (fill and spill) |
| `gwc` | mm/day | 0.01 … 5 | 0.5 | baseflow coefficient |
| `gwe` | &mdash; | 0.5 … 6 | 3 | baseflow exponent |
| `qc` | 1/day | 0.05 … 1 | 0.3 | overland linear-reservoir release rate |
| `lf` | &mdash; | 0 … 0.5 | 0.05 | fraction of routed flow lost at the outlet |
| `nshape` | &mdash; | 1 … 8 | 2 | Gamma unit-hydrograph shape |
| `kmult` | &mdash; | 0.1 … 4 | 0.6 | multiplier on the geomorphic UH scale |

### Optional tension-store extension

| name | units | range | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ptens` | &mdash; | 0 … 0.9 | 0.2 | fraction of soil storage that evaporates but cannot drain |
| `plp` | &mdash; | 0.05 … 1 | 0.6 | soil-moisture threshold below which ET is limited |
<!-- AUTOGEN:parameters END -->

Released sets may carry **widened ranges** for `hmaxaq`, `ft`, `gwe` and `b`;
the file records what it was fitted under and `config_from_meta` applies it. Do
not validate a released set against the defaults above.

## What is worth understanding

**`wm` and `b` are the runoff-generation pair.** CREST does not apply a
pointwise power law. Storage capacity is *distributed* across the unit with
shape `b`, and runoff is saturation excess integrated over that distribution —
the VIC variable-infiltration-capacity formulation. `wm` sets how much water the
unit holds on average; `b` sets how unevenly it is spread, and therefore how
much of the unit saturates for a given input. Large `b` means a long tail of
low-capacity area that produces runoff early, which reads as a flashy catchment.
This is the feature that keeps the formulation meaningful at sub-daily steps and
high rainfall intensity, where a lumped bucket would not be.

**`gwc`, `gwe` and `hmaxaq` are the baseflow triple.** Baseflow is
`gwc · expm1(gwe · GW / hmaxaq)` from an aquifer of finite capacity, not a linear
reservoir. It goes smoothly to zero as the aquifer empties, so a dry aquifer
needs no dead threshold and the gradient survives everywhere — which matters
when you are differentiating through the model. `gwe` controls how sharply
baseflow responds near full storage; `hmaxaq` is the scale it is measured
against, so the two trade off strongly and are hard to identify separately from
discharge alone.

**`nshape` and `kmult` are the routing pair.** The unit hydrograph is a Gamma
with shape `nshape` and a scale that `kmult` multiplies onto a geomorphic prior
derived from `area_km2`. The prior is what keeps `kmult` near 1 and
interpretable; without it the scale would have to be learned from nothing.
`kmult` is also the parameter that the legacy `dt/2` clamp silently killed — see
`examples/05_gradient_health.py`.

**`lf` is a sink, not a physical process.** It removes a fraction of routed flow
at the outlet and exists to absorb systematic volume error — a gauged area that
disagrees with the topographic polygon, an unmeasured diversion. Large fitted
`lf` is a signal to check the catchment's area, not a result.

**`ke` absorbs PET error.** All other forcings are fixed, so any bias in the PET
product has nowhere else to go. This matters when interpreting a calibrated set:
`ke` far from 1 says as much about the PET input as about the catchment.

## Optional: the tension store

`dcrest.BOUNDS_TENSION` adds the two parameters listed above, off by default.

`ptens` is the Sacramento tension-water construct: CREST drains soil water to
the aquifer in proportion to the whole storage, whereas SAC-SMA holds a tension
fraction that only evaporation can remove. Adding it is worth a small but very
robust gain on the CAMELS benchmark (paired ΔNSE +0.0025, seed-matched over six
seeds and both forcings, p ≈ 8e-32, with a dose-response in the fitted `ptens`).
`plp`, the HBV-style ET-efficiency threshold, gives nothing (−0.0002, p = 0.26).

The 16-parameter model remains the primary product, for continuity with EF5. The
extension quantifies what that piece of Sacramento structure is worth in CREST.
`default_parameters` and `CrestLumped` emit exactly the parameters in the
`bounds` you pass, so the extension can never change the base model by accident.

## Parameterisation for optimisation

`CrestLumped` stores unconstrained reals and maps them through a sigmoid into
the ranges above, so any `torch.optim` optimiser stays in bounds by
construction. `dcrest.params.to_raw` and `to_physical` convert between the two
if you need to move a parameter set between representations.
